client:
Honestly, I've been feeling really on edge since I lost my job last month. The uncertainty is eating at me - I keep worrying about how I'll pay rent next month if I don't find something soon. What if I can't get another tech job in this market? Everyone says the industry is tightening up. 

I'm not sure talking about it will help when what I really need is another paycheck. The job search just makes me feel more inadequate with every rejection.
therapist:
It sounds like you're carrying a heavy load of worry and self-doubt right now, especially with the financial pressure mounting. When those "what if" thoughts about the job market arise, have you noticed any patterns in how they affect your motivation to keep applying?

I hear you're feeling discouraged by the rejections - would it help to examine what evidence we might find that contradicts the thought "I'm inadequate"?

client:
I get what you're saying about looking for evidence, but honestly every rejection email just feels like proof that I'm not good enough. Like today when I got turned down from that junior developer position, all I could think was "See? Even entry-level jobs don't want me." 

It's hard to imagine what evidence would contradict that when the job market is so brutal right now. I've sent out over 50 applications and nothing's stuck.
therapist:
I hear how disheartening this feels, especially when each rejection seems to reinforce your doubts. Let's pause for a moment—when you read those rejection emails, what thoughts automatically come up about *why* they might have said no? 

Could we look at one of those applications together to see what skills and strengths you actually put forward?

client:
I immediately think they rejected me because I'm not good enough or qualified enough for the job. When I see those emails, I just feel like all my effort was wasted. Looking at my applications makes me anxious because it reminds me of all the times I've failed before. 

I don't know if going through one will help - I already know what I wrote, and it clearly wasn't good enough.
therapist:
It's understandable to feel this discouraged when your applications haven't yielded results yet—that disappointment is weighing heavily on you. The thought "all my effort was wasted" sounds particularly painful—have you noticed any small ways your applications or interview skills have improved through this process, even if the outcome hasn't changed yet?  

When anxiety makes you want to avoid looking at past applications, what would make it feel slightly safer to examine one together? We could focus just on noticing the facts rather than judging them.

client:
I guess I can see that my interview answers are getting a little smoother now that I've had more practice. But it just makes me more frustrated that I'm improving and still not getting offers. 

Looking at old applications feels like rubbing salt in the wound. What if I just see all the mistakes I made and realize I messed up my chances? That thought makes my chest feel tight.
therapist:
I hear how frustrating it is to see your skills improving yet still face rejection—that tightness in your chest tells me this hits on some deep fears. It takes real courage to keep practicing despite these setbacks.  

You mentioned noticing your interview answers getting smoother—can we focus on that improvement for a moment? What’s one small thing you’ve learned about presenting yourself better through this process?

client:
I guess I have gotten better at keeping my answers concise, but it doesn't seem to matter when they just don't like me as a person. I can tell the moment I walk in - their body language changes and I start panicking. It's like they can smell my desperation or something. 

All this practice just makes the rejections hurt more because I know I'm technically doing better, yet still failing. What's the point of improving when the outcome is always the same?
therapist:
It sounds like you're noticing real skill growth while also facing the painful disconnect when results don't follow—that combination can feel especially disheartening. When you mention interviewers' body language shifting, have you considered that what feels like "smelling desperation" to you might actually be your own anxiety influencing how you interpret their reactions?  

You're doing the hard work of improving despite the fear—what would it feel like to acknowledge that persistence as strength, even when the outcome isn't yet what you hope for?

client:
I get what you're saying about anxiety coloring my perception, but it's hard to believe that when I can physically see interviewers leaning back or checking the clock. It feels so concrete. And while I know I'm trying, calling it "strength" just makes me feel like I'm failing at being strong enough to actually land a job. 

The persistence just reminds me how long this has been going on without results—it's more exhausting than empowering right now.
therapist:
I hear how exhausting it is to keep pushing forward when the visible signs from interviewers seem to confirm your fears. That physical reaction you notice—the leaning back, clock-checking—must make it incredibly hard to stay present in those moments.  

When you're in the thick of an interview and notice those cues, what's one small grounding technique you've tried or might try to recenter yourself? Even something as simple as feeling your feet on the floor—not to change their reaction, but to steady your own.

client: I've tried focusing on my breathing before, but in the moment it just makes me more aware of how nervous I am. When I see the interviewer lean back or check the clock, my mind immediately jumps to "they hate me" and then everything spirals from there. The physical grounding techniques feel too simple to counteract that overwhelming panic.
therapist:
It makes complete sense that focusing on your breathing would heighten your awareness of the nervousness when you're already in that spiral of "they hate me"—that thought carries such a visceral punch.  

When that panic starts to take over, what if we approached it differently? Instead of trying to calm the physical symptoms first, what happens if you name the thought explicitly—like actually saying to yourself "I'm having the thought that they hate me"—to create just a sliver of distance from it?

client:
I get what you're saying about creating distance from the thought, but when I'm in that panicked state, it feels so real and immediate. Saying it out loud almost makes it more concrete, like I'm admitting something terrible is true. 

I've tried similar techniques before and they just made me feel more self-conscious, like now I'm not just anxious but also talking to myself like a crazy person. Does that make sense?
therapist:
I hear how those techniques can sometimes amplify the self-consciousness rather than help in the moment—that makes complete sense when you're already feeling exposed. The fear of seeming "crazy" to yourself adds another layer to an already overwhelming experience.  

Since naming the thought aloud feels too intense right now, what if we experimented with simply noticing the panic as a temporary wave—without trying to change it or judge it? Not as a solution, but just to observe how long it actually lasts when you don't fight it.

client:
I get what you're saying about not fighting the panic, but it's so hard not to judge it when it feels like my whole body is screaming that something's wrong. The other day at the grocery store, I had to abandon my cart and leave because the wave just kept getting bigger—it didn't feel temporary at all. 

I worry that if I just observe it without trying to stop it, I'll lose control completely. What if the wave never actually passes? That's my biggest fear.
therapist:
That grocery store experience sounds terrifying—when your body's screaming that you're in danger, it's completely understandable that observing rather than reacting would feel impossible. That fear of losing control makes perfect sense when the panic *feels* endless in the moment.  

When you recall that incident now, can you notice any small signs that the wave *did* eventually pass—even if it took leaving the situation? I wonder what might happen if we gently explored that gap between how long the panic *feels* versus how long it *actually* lasts.

client:
I guess it did pass eventually, but that doesn’t make it any less awful in the moment. The worst part is how long it *feels*—like time just stretches out forever. Even remembering it now makes my chest tight. 

I don’t know if focusing on how long it actually lasted helps, because in that state, logic just doesn’t reach me. It’s like my brain short-circuits.
therapist:
I hear how the sheer intensity of those moments makes logic feel useless in the moment—that short-circuit feeling is so visceral when you're in it. You're absolutely right that knowing it'll pass doesn't make the experience less awful *while it's happening*.  

Since logic feels inaccessible then, what if we explored just one physical anchor—something external you could focus on (like the cold of a water bottle or texture of a keychain) to tether you slightly when time feels distorted? Not to stop the panic, just to give your brain one small "outside" signal to notice.
